name: Conceptual schematic
summary: A cartoon of activation space or of an argument, drawn where the paper has a claim but no measurement for it yet. Its job is to fix what a hypothesis means, or what would count as evidence for one, so the reader can hold the picture against the measured figures that follow.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Each of these four drawings sits where the paper has a claim but no number for it. Figure 3 states what the observed network is supposed to *be* under [[superposition]] — the hypothesis that a network represents more [[feature|features]] (interpretable directions in activation space) than it has neurons, giving each a direction rather than a neuron of its own. Figure 7 states, before any evidence appears, what would count as ruling out [[polysemanticity]]: a single unit firing on clearly unrelated things. Figure 45 states what the geometry of [[feature-splitting]] ought to look like. Figure 62 asks whether a feature is a single direction at all.

Bar charts, averages and tables all need an axis with units and a population to aggregate over. These four claims contain a relation instead: inside or outside, more or fewer, same territory or new, one description or two. Putting a number to any would misreport its status — figure 3 imports a hypothesis from earlier work, and figure 62 is conjecture the text marks with "perhaps". A cartoon wears that on its face; a plot would hide it.

### How to read it, step by step

There are no axes. Start with the sentence printed beside or below the drawing — the words carry the claim, the picture only stages it. Then find what changes between panels; that difference is the argument, the rest is scaffolding.

The vocabulary is small and reused. A dot is one unit: a neuron in figure 3, a token where a feature fires in figure 7, a [[feature-direction]] (the unit vector a feature writes along) in figures 45 and 62. An arrow is either a mapping — figure 3's dashed orange arrows point downward, meaning the large network is expressed inside the small one, not recovered from it — or a direction from the origin, as in figure 45, where every arrow shares a tail because only angles mean anything.

Colour is load-bearing. Orange marks the operative element: the projection in figure 3, the boundary of the [[computational-proxy]] in figure 7 — a score $\log(P(s\mid\text{context})/P(s))$ computed from the text alone, independent of the autoencoder. Grey means backdrop or conjecture: figure 45's faint arrows are the paper's imagined [[true-features]], fixed in all three panels so you watch the bold learned ones multiply against them.

Then stop. Counting dots or reading positions as coordinates invents precision the drawing lacks: figure 3's six-into-three squeeze stands in for 4,096 features over 512 neurons, and figure 62's ring carries four points because four space evenly.

### What a bad result would look like

Two of them draw the failure themselves. Figure 7's first panel *is* the bad case — dots scattered across the circle with no shared region; the paper's example is a neuron of this transformer that fires on academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean text. That is a failure of [[activation-specificity]]. Figure 62's left panel deflates its own hypothesis: a "manifold" that is only the convex hull of features firing together is [[correlated-features]] renamed, not a rival account.

The other two you construct. Figure 3 fails if each neuron already is one clean feature — a sufficient [[privileged-basis]] — which would leave [[dictionary-learning]] nothing to do. Figure 45 fails if widening the [[sparse-autoencoder]] throws the bold arrows outside the grey blob, or to wide angles from each other: new territory rather than finer division, and the UMAP behind it would show no tight clusters. Neither can be settled by looking; falsification lives in the measured figures each schematic points at.

### Where it comes back

What changes across the four is distance from evidence. Figure 3 opens the problem setup on borrowed ground. Figure 7 sets the standard the case studies are then held to, and its third panel already concedes that features are often narrower than the proxy, so several share its region ([[multiple-features-for-one-context]]). Figure 45 arrives *after* the UMAP that measured it — a cartoon of a result, not an announcement. Figure 62 sits in the discussion with no experiment behind it, offered as one reason splitting never stopped at any width tried, and why the [[correct-number-of-features]] may not be well posed.
